pharm: Cobalamin coenzyme; cofactor for methionine synthase and methyl-group metabolism
quick: Oral 500-1500 mcg/day; IM 500-1000 mcg as per deficiency protocol
May take with or without food
Safe at recommended doses; required nutrient
Chronic alcohol may impair B12 status
B12 level, CBC, homocysteine, neurologic response
summary: Methylcobalamin is the active, methylated form of vitamin B12 used to treat and prevent B12 deficiency and associated megaloblastic anemia and peripheral neuropathy. It is well tolerated with very low toxicity. It is essential for DNA synthesis, myelin formation, and homocysteine metabolism.
indications: Vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia
Prevention/treatment of B12 deficiency in vegetarians, malabsorption, post-gastrectomy

dosage.d: 500-1000 mcg on alternate days for 1-2 weeks, then 500-1000 mcg every 1-3 months for maintenance
dosage.n: Higher initial frequency for neurological involvement
High-dose oral can substitute for IM in many patients

dosage.d: 1500 mcg/day oral, or 500-1000 mcg IM 1-3 times weekly
dosage.n: Often combined with other neurotropic B vitamins

dosage.d: Dose per age and severity under specialist guidance

admin: Oral tablets/sublingual: take with or without food
IM injection: deep intramuscular; protect from light during handling
Identify and address the cause of deficiency (diet, malabsorption, drugs)
Check baseline B12, CBC, and folate before treatment of anemia
Avoid giving folic acid alone in B12 deficiency (masks anemia, neuropathy progresses)
moa: Serves as a coenzyme for methionine synthase, transferring a methyl group to convert homocysteine to methionine and regenerate tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis. This supports normal erythropoiesis and is essential for myelin synthesis and maintenance of neuronal function.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to cobalamin or cobalt
Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (cobalamin can worsen optic atrophy)
relative: Concurrent unexplained anemia until cause established
monitor: Hematologic response and potassium during correction of severe anemia

preg: Considered safe and necessary during pregnancy at recommended dietary/therapeutic doses; B12 deficiency itself harms fetal development. No evidence of harm from supplementation.
lact: Safe and recommended; vitamin B12 is a normal milk constituent and supplementation supports infant stores. Important in exclusively breastfed infants of B12-deficient mothers.
renal: No dose adjustment for usual supplementation; water-soluble with renal excretion of excess. Safe in renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment required; well tolerated in hepatic impairment.

major: None clinically significant at recommended doses
moderate: Metformin (long-term reduces B12 absorption - increases requirement)
Proton pump inhibitors / H2 blockers (reduce B12 absorption)
minor: Excess folic acid can mask hematologic B12 deficiency
interactions.food: Dietary B12 from animal sources; well absorbed; no significant adverse food interaction
interactions.alcohol: Chronic heavy alcohol use impairs absorption and may worsen deficiency
interactions.diagnostics: Supplementation normalizes serum B12 and may correct elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; can mask underlying folate-deficient megaloblastosis

serious: Hypokalemia during rapid correction of severe megaloblastic anemia

monitoring: Serum potassium during early correction of severe anemia
Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid if assessing functional status
counsel: Take consistently; lifelong therapy may be needed in pernicious anemia or malabsorption
Vegetarians/vegans and long-term metformin or acid-suppressant users should supplement
Report palpitations or weakness during treatment of severe anemia
Do not rely on folic acid alone if B12 deficient
Identify and treat the cause of deficiency with your clinician
pk: Oral plasma peak within 1-2 hours; IM rapid
Body stores cycle over years; plasma clearance variable
Long; hepatic stores last months to years
Store below 25-30°C, protect from light; keep injection away from light
pearls: Methylcobalamin is a coenzyme form that does not require conversion, often preferred for neuropathy
High-dose oral B12 (1000-2000 mcg/day) is effective even in pernicious anemia via passive absorption
Always check folate and treat both; never give folate alone in B12 deficiency
Watch for hypokalemia in the first days of treating severe megaloblastic anemia
Long-term metformin and PPIs are common iatrogenic causes of B12 deficiency
missed: Take a missed oral dose when remembered, unless it is near the next dose; do not double up. For maintenance injections, reschedule the missed dose with your clinician.
overdose: Vitamin B12 has very low toxicity; excess is excreted renally. No specific toxic syndrome or antidote; supportive care only. Very high parenteral doses may rarely cause hypersensitivity.
